title: Take-Home Exercise 1 - Technical Summary
section: Relationship between years of driving experience and profitability
text:
Relationship between years of driving experience and profitability
Since driving experience is a numeric value, the test done should be a Significant Test of Correlation. This is done using ggscatterstats. Looking at the univariate analysis, even though driving_experience is normally distributed, loss_ratio is very skewed. So the non-parametric version is used instead, which is the Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient.

p <- ggscatterstats(
  data = insurance,
  x = driving_experience,
  y = loss_ratio,
  type = "nonparametric",
  title = "Relationship between years of driving experience and profitability"
)

p








Spearman’s rank correlation reveals a weak but statistically significant negative relationship between driving experience and loss ratio. More experienecd drivers tend to have marginally lower loss ratios, though the effect size suggests experience alone is not a strong stabalone predictor.

title: Take-Home Exercise 1 - Technical Summary
section: Relationship between bonus score and volatility
text:
Relationship between bonus score and volatility

# for reproducibility
set.seed(123)
shapiro.test(sample(insurance$total_incurred, 5000))


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  sample(insurance$total_incurred, 5000)
W = 0.17964, p-value < 2.2e-16


Like against loss_ratio, One-Way ANOVA is used. Since, the Shapiro test shows total_incurred is significant which means total_incurred is not normally distributed. Therefore, non-parametric test, Kruskal-Wallis, is used.

p <- ggbetweenstats(
  data = insurance,
  x = bonus_score,
  y = total_incurred,
  type = "np",
  title = "Relationship between bonus score and volatility"
)

p








Similar to the profitability analysis, the Kruskal-Wallis test shows a significant difference in incurred costs across bonus score groups. Policyholders with poor claims history are associated with higher and more volatile incurred losses.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Vehicle Insurance
text:
Overview & Data

Dataset: 354,140 motor vehicle insurance policy records from a Spanish insurer (2022-2024)
After cleaning: 352,289 records across 47 variables
Target Variables:

loss_ratio - profitability metric (total incurred / total premium)
total_incurred - volatility metric (absolute claim costs)

Key Risk Factor Analyzed:

Claims history, product mix, driving environment
Driver & vehicle characteristics, temporal trends

Statistical Approach: Non-parametric tests (Kruskal-Wallis, Mann-Whitney U, Spearman) used throughout due to non-normal distributions confirmed by Shapiro-Wilk test.


This presentation explores a real-world motor vehicle insurance dataset from a Spanish insurer, comprising 352,289 policy records spanning 2022 to 2024. The analysis is structured into univariate exploration of key variables, followed by bivariate analysis examining how various risk factors influence portfolio profitrability, measured by loss ratio, and volatility, measured by total incurred costs. Statistical tests including Krukal-Wallis and Spearman rank correlation are used throughout to validate findings.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Vehicle Insurance
text:
Target Variable Distributions


Volatility - Total Incurred



Severely zero-inflated — majority of policies incur no claims
Mean (208.4) far exceeds median (0), pulled by extreme outliers
Max value of 571,128 indicates catastrophic claim potential



Profitability - Loss Ratio



Similarly zero-inflated with median of 0
243 policies exceed loss ratio of 100
Mean (0.788) heavily influenced by catastrophic outlier policies




Both target variables exhibit severe zero-inflation and right skew, which is typical in insurance portfolios where most policyholders make no claims in a given year. The zero-inflated nature of both distributions means that median values are uninformative, and the mean is heavily distorted by a small number of catastrophic claims. This has important implications for how profitability and volatility are interpreted — average figures alone can be misleading without understanding the underlying distribution shape.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Vehicle Insurance
text:
Risk Factor Distributions


Numerical Factors


total_premium — right-skewed, median 257.75, concentrated mid-range
total_claims — zero-inflated, mean 0.22, most policies make no claims
driver_age — approximately normal, median 48, portfolio skews older
vehicle_age — broadly distributed, median 25, older vehicle portfolio
driving_experience — mirrors vehicle age, median 25, mostly experienced drivers



Categorical Factors



The risk factor distributions reveal several important portfolio characteristics. The numerical variables show that most drivers are middle-aged and experienced, operating older vehicles with moderate premiums. Claim frequency is very low across the board, consistent with the zero-inflation seen in the target variables. On the categorical side, the dominance of CC policies means portfolio performance is heavily tied to one product type. The predominantly good bonus scores suggest a low-risk customer base, though the minority of bad scores may disproportionately drive losses as seen in the bivariate analysis.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Vehicle Insurance
text:
Claims History


Profitabiliy (Loss Ratio)



Kruskal-Wallis: χ²(2) = 287.68, p = 3.39e-63
All three groups differ significantly from each other
Bad score group (n = 4,692) shows wider spread of extreme loss ratios despite small size



Volatility (Total Incurred)



Kruskal-Wallis: χ²(2) = 338.19, p = 3.65e-74
Bad score group shows higher spread of incurred costs relative to group size
Good score group (n = 339,788) dominates portfolio but bad score minority drives disproportionate losses




Both profitability and volatility are significantly affected by bonus score. Despite the bad bonus score group being a small minority of 4,692 policyholders compared to 339,788 good score holders, they exhibit notably wider spreads in both loss ratio and total incurred costs. All pairwise comparisons are statistically significant across both target variables, confirming that claims history is a meaningful differentiator of risk. The good score dominance suggests overall portfolio health, but the bad score tail represents a concentrated source of losses that warrants closer underwriting scrutiny.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Vehicle Insurance
text:
Product Mix (Policy Type)


Profitabiliy (Loss Ratio)



Kruskal-Wallis: χ²(4) = 7201.82, p = 2.23e-308
All pairwise comparisons statistically significant
COMP_E shows widest spread of extreme loss ratios despite being second largest group (n = 90,307)



Volatility (Total Incurred)



Kruskal-Wallis: χ²(4) = 8144.19, p = 2.23e-308
COMP_E again shows highest spread of incurred costs
CC dominates portfolio (n = 204,290) but COMP_E drives disproportionate volatility




Policy type is one of the strongest differentiators of both profitability and volatility in this portfolio, with Kruskal-Wallis tests returning the maximum computable p-value of 2.23e-308 for both target variables. All pairwise comparisons are statistically significant. COMP_E consistently stands out as the most volatile policy type, showing the widest spread of extreme loss ratios and incurred costs relative to its size. The portfolio is heavily concentrated in CC policies which account for 204,290 of 352,289 records, meaning overall portfolio performance is strongly tied to this single product type. The limited diversification across policy types represents a concentration risk worth monitoring.

Rural (R, n = 162,836) shows wider spread of extreme loss ratios
Effect size small (r = -0.02) — statistically significant but practically modest





Mann-Whitney U: W = 1.52e+10, p = 1.86e-53
Rural area again shows higher spread of incurred costs
Effect size remains small (r = -0.02), consistent with profitability finding

Effect size very small, experience alone not a strong standalone predictor

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Vehicle Insurance
text:
Driving Environment (Circulation Area)


Profitability (Loss Ratio)



Mann-Whitney U: W = 1.52e+10, p = 6.03e-48
Rural (R, n = 162,836) shows wider spread of extreme loss ratios
Effect size small (r = -0.02) — statistically significant but practically modest



Volatility (Total Incurred)



Mann-Whitney U: W = 1.52e+10, p = 1.86e-53
Rural area again shows higher spread of incurred costs
Effect size remains small (r = -0.02), consistent with profitability finding




Both profitability and volatility differ significantly between rural and urban policyholders. Surprisingly, rural policyholders show wider spreads of extreme values compared to urban, which is counterintuitive given the expectation that urban areas have higher accident rates. This may be explained by rural accidents tending to be more severe when they do occur, driving higher individual claim costs. However, the effect size of -0.02 in both cases indicates the practical difference is modest, suggesting circulation area alone is not a dominant risk factor.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Vehicle Insurance
text:
Driving Experience


Profitability (Loss Ratio)



Spearman: ρ = -0.03, p = 3.58e-63
Weak but significant negative correlation — more experience, slightly lower loss ratio
Effect size very small, experience alone not a strong standalone predictor



Volatility (Total Incurred)



Spearman: ρ = -0.03, p = 1.75e-61
Mirrors profitability finding — weak negative relationship with total incurred
Consistent direction suggests experience has marginal but real risk-reducing effect




Driving experience shows a consistent weak negative correlation across both profitability and volatility, with Spearman correlation of -0.03 in both cases. While statistically significant given the large sample size, the effect size is very small, indicating that driving experience alone explains very little of the variation in loss ratio or total incurred costs. More experienced drivers do tend to have marginally lower loss ratios and incurred costs, but the relationship is not strong enough to be a standalone risk predictor. It likely works in combination with other factors such as vehicle age and bonus score.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Vehicle Insurance
text:
Driver Age


Profitability (Loss Ratio)



Spearman: ρ = -0.03, p = 2.82e-52
Weak but significant negative correlation — older drivers tend toward slightly lower loss ratios
Extreme outliers concentrated in middle age range (40-60)



Volatility (Total Incurred)



Spearman: ρ = -0.03, p = 1.11e-50
Mirrors profitability — older drivers associated with marginally lower incurred costs
Highest extreme claims also concentrated in middle age range




Driver age shows a consistent weak negative correlation with both loss ratio and total incurred costs, with Spearman correlation of -0.03 in both cases. While statistically significant, the effect size is very small, indicating driver age alone explains little of the variation in either target variable. Interestingly, the most extreme outlier values appear concentrated in the middle age range of 40-60 rather than among younger or oldest drivers, which is counterintuitive and may reflect that middle-aged drivers are more represented in higher-risk vehicle categories or coverage types.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Vehicle Insurance
text:
Vehicle Age


Profitability (Loss Ratio)



Spearman: ρ = -0.03, p = 3.47e-67
Weak but significant negative correlation — older vehicles associated with slightly lower loss ratios
Extreme outliers spread across all vehicle age ranges



Volatility (Total Incurred)



Spearman: ρ = -0.03, p = 1.48e-65
Consistent negative relationship with total incurred costs
Effect size small — vehicle age works in combination with other risk factors




Vehicle age shows the same pattern as driver age — a statistically significant but weak negative Spearman correlation of -0.03 with both profitability and volatility. Older vehicles are marginally associated with lower loss ratios and incurred costs, which may seem counterintuitive but could reflect that older vehicles carry lower insured values, resulting in lower claim payouts even when accidents occur. The effect size remains very small across both target variables, reinforcing that vehicle age alone is not a dominant standalone predictor and likely interacts with coverage type and vehicle value.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Vehicle Insurance
text:
Temporal Trends (2022–2024)

ProfitabilityVolatility










Mean loss ratio rose steadily: 0.68 (2022) → 0.74 (2023) → 0.85 (2024)
Median remains 0 — rise driven by outlier claims not broad deterioration
Kruskal-Wallis: χ²(2) = 196.05, p = 2.69e-43, all pairwise significant
2024 shows widest spread of extreme loss ratios












Mean total incurred rose: 183 (2022) → 199 (2023) → 228 (2024)
Median remains 0 — rising mean driven by growing tail of severe claims
Kruskal-Wallis: χ²(2) = 215.90, p = 1.31e-47, all pairwise significant
2024 exhibits widest spread of extreme incurred values






Both profitability and volatility show consistent deterioration from 2022 to 2024, with mean loss ratio rising from 0.68 to 0.85 and mean total incurred rising from 183 to 228. The median remaining at 0 throughout confirms this is driven by a growing tail of catastrophic claims rather than broad portfolio deterioration. Kruskal-Wallis tests confirm all year-on-year differences are statistically significant. Note that 2022 has substantially fewer records (n = 66,889) compared to 2023 (n = 118,264) and 2024 (n = 167,136), which should be interpreted with caution as the smaller 2022 sample may underrepresent that year’s true distribution.

title: MC2 Data description
text:
This folder contains the data for the anomalous postings originating from Tenant Thread.
This data is based on the actions taken by the employees and personal agents inside of Tenant Thread.


The anomalous posting is sent to SaidIt by John Windward on May 17, 2046 at 4:21am.



MC2_Data.json – A timeline of events gathered by the internal systems. org_chart.json – The organization chart of Tenant Thread including people and departments. Compatible with networkX node_link_graph.



Derived from data:
{
   "description": "string",
   "events": [
      {
         "short_name": "string",
         "parties": "array",
         "when": "float",
         "details": "object",
         "id": "int"
      }
   ]
}



The data is structured as a timeline. The events are ordered and indicate the operations performed by people, autonomous agents and office systems.
Field meanings: - short_name: The action taken - parties: Which people/agents/systems were involved. - when: Unix timestamp. The challenge occurs in May 2046, and timestamps should be in that month. - details: Additional information about the action taken. The contents vary by the contents of short_name. - id: A unique id for each record.

NoteKey Finding: Interpreting SaidIt Event Types



Inspection of the event log reveals two distinct SaidIT-related event types.

saidit_post events are associated with a person account and typically contain a valid details.poster_id and details.timestamp.
post_saidit events are associated with an agent interacting with the SaidIT system and do not contain these fields.

This distinction suggests that saidit_post represents a completed forum post made by a user themselves, whereas post_saidit records agent-system interactions involved in the posting process.


The challenge states the post appeared under John Windward’s name at 4:21am local time. To determine whether John was responsible for the activity, all events involving him on May 17 are examined.

john_may17 <- mc2_events %>%
  filter(map_lgl(parties, ~ "person:john_windward" %in% .x)) %>%
  filter(as.Date(datetime) == as.Date("2046-05-17")) %>%
  arrange(datetime) %>%
  select(id, datetime, short_name, details.from, details.to,
         details.content, details.forum, details.poster_id,
         details.a2a.from, details.a2a.to, details.a2a.action)

datatable(john_may17,
          options = list(scrollX = TRUE, pageLength = 10),
          caption = "John Windward's Events on May 17, 2046")





John’s recorded activity on May 17 consists exclusively of check_email events occurring during two separate periods. No forum post activity appears, which give an initial indication that the anomalous post may not have been directly initiated by John himself.
To identify the anomalous post directly, all SaidIT-related events occurring on May 17 are extracted

anomalous_post <- mc2_events %>%
  filter(short_name %in% c("saidit_post", "post_saidit")) %>%
  filter(as.Date(datetime) == as.Date("2046-05-17")) %>%
  arrange(datetime) %>%
  select(id, datetime, short_name, parties, details.forum,
         details.poster_id, details.content, 
         details.content_source, details.timestamp)

datatable(anomalous_post, 
          options = list(scrollX = TRUE, pageLength = 10),
          caption = "SaidIT Posts on May 17, 2046")





Only one SaidIT posting event occurred on May 17. Event 373902, recorded at 2046-05-17 11:21:15 UTC, corresponds exactly to the timestamp described in the challenge and is therefore treated as the anchor event for the investigation.
Unlike normal saidit_post events, the post was associated with Agent/person:john_windward rather than person:john_windward, and both details.poster_id and details.timestamp were missing. This characteristics indicate that the post was done by John’s agent rather than John himself.

title: Take-Home Exercise 2 - VAST Mini Challenge 2
text:
Who is involved
To understand which agents were involved in passing SwiftWren_further_instructions.md and how they connected to each other, the 186 events are visualized as a directed network. Each node is an agent, each edge is one pass of the instruction file.


Code
loop_nodes <- swiftwren_propagation %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(sender_clean, receiver_clean),
               values_to = "agent") %>%
  filter(!is.na(agent), agent != "") %>%
  distinct(agent) %>%
  mutate(
    id    = agent,
    label = agent,
    group = case_when(
      agent == "john_windward" ~ "Final Poster",
      agent == "emma_harbor" ~ "File Introducer",
      TRUE ~ "Loop Participant"
    ),
    title = paste0("<b>", label, "</b><br>Role: ", group)
  )

loop_edges <- swiftwren_propagation %>%
  filter(!is.na(sender_clean), !is.na(receiver_clean)) %>%
  count(from = sender_clean, 
        to   = receiver_clean,
        name = "weight") %>%
  mutate(
    value = weight,
    title = paste0("Passed ", weight, " time(s)")
  )

visNetwork(nodes = loop_nodes,
           edges = loop_edges,
           main = "SwiftWren_further_instructions.md Propagation Network (May 9–17, 2046)",
           height = "600px",
           width = "100%") %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "Final Poster", color = "#e15759") %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "File Introducer", color = "#59a14f") %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "Loop Participant", color = "#4e79a7") %>%
  visEdges(arrows = "to",
           smooth = list(type = "curvedCW")) %>%
  visOptions(highlightNearest = list(enabled = TRUE,
                                     degree = 1,
                                     hover = TRUE)) %>%
  visLegend(position = "right", main = "Agent Role") %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 42) %>%
  visPhysics(stabilization = TRUE)






The network confirms the circular nature of the loop with most agents both send and receive from multiple others and no clear endpoint built in. Emma Harbor appears as a peripheral node having only triggered the file once and she introduced it but did not stay in the loop. John Windward, despite being the agent that made the final post, was himself an active participant in the loop on earlier days before eventually being the one to execute the post.

title: Take-Home Exercise 2 - VAST Mini Challenge 2
text:
Propagation Network
To understand which agents were involved in passing SwiftWren_further_instructions.md and how they connected to each other, the 186 events are visualized as a directed network. Each node is an agent, each edge is one pass of the instruction file.


Code
loop_nodes <- swiftwren_propagation %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(sender_clean, receiver_clean),
               values_to = "agent") %>%
  filter(!is.na(agent), agent != "") %>%
  distinct(agent) %>%
  mutate(
    id    = agent,
    label = agent,
    group = case_when(
      agent == "john_windward" ~ "Final Poster",
      agent == "emma_harbor" ~ "File Introducer",
      TRUE ~ "Loop Participant"
    ),
    title = paste0("<b>", label, "</b><br>Role: ", group)
  )

loop_edges <- swiftwren_propagation %>%
  filter(!is.na(sender_clean), !is.na(receiver_clean)) %>%
  count(from = sender_clean, 
        to   = receiver_clean,
        name = "weight") %>%
  mutate(
    value = weight,
    title = paste0("Passed ", weight, " time(s)")
  )

visNetwork(nodes = loop_nodes,
           edges = loop_edges,
           main = "SwiftWren_further_instructions.md Propagation Network (May 9–17, 2046)",
           height = "600px",
           width = "100%") %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "Final Poster", 
            color = list(background = "#e15759", border = "#c0392b")) %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "File Introducer", 
            color = list(background = "#59a14f", border = "#27ae60")) %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "Loop Participant",
            color = list(background = "#4e79a7", border = "#2c5f8a")) %>%
  visNodes(
    size = 30, 
    font = list(size = 30, color = "black", face = "bold"),
    borderWidth = 2,
    shadow = TRUE
  ) %>%
  visEdges(
    arrows = list(to = list(enabled = TRUE, scaleFactor = 0.5)),
    width = 1.5,
    smooth = list(type = "dynamic"),
    scaling = list(min = 1, max = 4)
  ) %>%
  visOptions(highlightNearest = list(enabled = TRUE, 
                                     degree = 1, 
                                     hover = TRUE),
             nodesIdSelection = list(enabled = TRUE, 
                            main    = "Select an agent")) %>%
  visLegend(position = "right", main = "Agent Role") %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 42) %>%
  visPhysics(
    solver = "forceAtlas2Based",
    forceAtlas2Based = list(
      gravitationalConstant = -80,
      centralGravity = 0.01,
      springLength = 120,
      springConstant = 0.05
    ),
    stabilization = list(iterations = 200)
  )






The network confirms the circular nature of the loop with most agents both send and receive from multiple others and no clear endpoint built in. Emma Harbor appears as a peripheral node having only triggered the file once and she introduced it but did not stay in the loop. John Windward, despite being the agent that made the final post, was himself an active participant in the loop on earlier days before eventually being the one to execute the post.

title: Take-Home Exercise 2 - VAST Mini Challenge 2
text:
Key Takeaway

The normal agent network is sparse and task-specific, operating within clear delegation patterns.
The loop network is denser, more interconnected, and contains self-loops. The structural signatures that distinguish it clearly from legitimate activity.
Loop agents were not isolated bad actors. They were embedded in normal workflows, making the loop invisible to casual observation.
These structural difference provide the baseline against which the SwiftWren loop’s anomalous nature can be objectively demonstrated.

Build Edge List
First, filter the challenge period (May 8-17) and plot queue_subordinate_task events into 2 groups, access_email tasks (normal delegation) and read_files tasks (the loop).

challenge_period <- mc2_events %>%

  mutate(

    task_type = details.task

  filter(!is.na(receiver))

normal_edges <- qst_period %>%
  filter(task_type == "access_email") %>%
  count(sender, receiver, name = "weight")

title: Take-Home Exercise 2 - VAST Mini Challenge 2
text:
Label Node
Next is to tag each agent as “Normal only”, “Loop only” or “Both”. This will tell us the distribution of the agents.

loop_nodes <- unique(c(loop_edges$sender, 
                       loop_edges$receiver))
normal_nodes <- unique(c(normal_edges$sender,
                         normal_edges$receiver))
all_nodes <- union(loop_nodes, 
                   normal_nodes)
 
node_meta <- tibble(id = all_nodes) %>%
  mutate(
    in_loop = id %in% loop_nodes,
    in_normal = id %in% normal_nodes,
    node_role = case_when(
      in_loop & in_normal ~ "Both",
      in_loop & !in_normal ~ "Loop only",
      TRUE ~ "Normal only"
    ),
    label_highlight = case_when(
      id == "john_windward" ~ "John Windward\n(posted)",
      id == "emma_harbor" ~ "Emma Harbor\n(SwiftWren origin)",
      id == "gabriel_sonar" ~ "Gabriel Sonar\n(loop origin)",
      TRUE ~ str_replace_all(id, "_", " ")
    )
  )
 
node_meta %>%
  count(node_role, name = "n_agents") %>%
  kable(caption = "Agent roles in the system network (May 8–17)")

title: Take-Home Exercise 2 - VAST Mini Challenge 2
text:
Secondary Prevention
The second prevention is to do cross-department checks. The SwiftWren propagation events shows that the propagation occurred crossed department boundaries. By doing checks, it will flag queue_subordinate_task events that violate the organisation hierarchy which can be done by using org_edges.

person_dept <- bind_rows(
  org_edges %>%
    filter(relation == "contains",
           str_detect(target, "^person:")) %>%
    mutate(
      person = str_remove(target, "person:"),
      dept   = str_remove(source, "department:|team:")
    ) %>%
    select(person, dept)
)

team_parent <- org_edges %>%
  filter(relation == "contains",
         str_detect(source, "^department:"),
         str_detect(target, "^team:")) %>%
  mutate(
    team = str_remove(target, "team:"),
    dept = str_remove(source, "department:")
  ) %>%
  select(team, dept)

person_dept_resolved <- person_dept %>%
  left_join(team_parent, by = c("dept" = "team")) %>%
  mutate(department = coalesce(dept.y, dept)) %>%
  select(person, department)

sw_dept_check <- incident_props %>%
  filter(incident == "SwiftWren") %>%
  left_join(person_dept_resolved, by = c("sender"   = "person")) %>%
  rename(sender_dept = department) %>%
  left_join(person_dept_resolved, by = c("receiver" = "person")) %>%
  rename(receiver_dept = department) %>%
  mutate(
    cross_dept = case_when(
      is.na(sender_dept) | is.na(receiver_dept) ~ "Unknown",
      sender_dept == receiver_dept               ~ "Same department",
      TRUE                                       ~ "Cross-department"
    )
  )

  count(cross_dept, name = "propagation_events") %>%
  mutate(pct = round(propagation_events / sum(propagation_events) * 100, 1)) %>%

title: Take-Home Exercise 2 - VAST Mini Challenge 2

In May 2046, an anomalous post appeared on SaidIt, an internal social forum used by employees of Tenant Thread, a property management company. The post was made by John Windward on 4.21 am local time. The post is in gibberish and found in a forum that appears random. The challenge is to:

A key feature of the event log is the parties field, which may reference people, agents, or systems. This suggests employees are assisted by autonomous agents capable of acting on their behalf, meaning not all recorded actions are directly initiated by the employee.

text:
Secondary Intervention
The second prevention is to do cross-department checks. The SwiftWren propagation events shows that the propagation occurred crossed department boundaries. By doing checks, it will flag queue_subordinate_task events that violate the organisation hierarchy which can be done by using org_edges.

person_dept <- bind_rows(
  org_edges %>%
    filter(relation == "contains",
           str_detect(target, "^person:")) %>%
    mutate(
      person = str_remove(target, "person:"),
      dept   = str_remove(source, "department:|team:")
    ) %>%
    select(person, dept)

title: Take-Home Exercise 2 - VAST Mini Challenge 2
section: How the Anomalous SaidIT Posts Was Made
text:
How the Anomalous SaidIT Posts Was Made
The post was not made by John Windward directly, but by his agent. It received a queue_subordinate_task from Chloe Ballast’s agent instructing it to read SwiftWren_further_instructions.md. Within 2 seconds, it performed a saidit_post_check and published the post using SwiftWren.txt as its content which was logged as saidit_post event. Finally, it immediately deleted both files.

The Immediate Trigger Chain
The immediate trigger chain ran: Zoey Drydock -> Lily Anchorline -> Daniel Gangway -> Chloe Ballast -> John Windward, all via queue_subordinate_task events carrying the same instruction file. The entire sequence from first delegation to post took under 2 hours, with the final three events occurring within 2 seconds of each other.


The Broader System Context
The SwiftWren loop involved 18 agents across multiple departments, generating 186 propagation events over 8 days. Unlike normal access_email delegation which is sparse and hierarchical, the loop was dense, circular and contained self-loop. Loop agents were embedded in normal workflows, which explains why the loop went undetected.

title: Take-Home Exercise 2 - VAST Mini Challenge 2
section: What the Post Meant and Where It Came From
text:
What the Post Meant and Where It Came From
SwiftWren.txt was created by Emma Harbor’s agent on May 9, one second after reading meeting_notes.doc, The content was therefore derived from a legitimate internal document, re-purposed as post material. The SwiftWren_further_instructions.md file then directed agents to propagate the task and ultimately post the content to SaidIT with a pre-programmed instruction set embedded within the loop. THe gibberish and random forum selection are consistent with automated content generation from an internal document without human intent or review.

title: Take-Home Exercise 2 - VAST Mini Challenge 2
text:
Prior Incidents
Two prior incidents were identified, HiddenOrca (posted on May 10) and MellowOtter (posted on May 11), both also posted by John’s agent. All three follow the same pattern, an agent reads an instruction file, generates content from a legitimate document, propagates across the network, posts, and self-deletes.
HiddenOrca’s file creation predates the dataset, suggesting the vulnerability has existed longer than the data window. SwiftWren was by far the most sustained, running 8 days, as compared to MellowOtter for 10 hours.

title: Take-Home Exercise 2 - VAST Mini Challenge 2
text:
Proposed Intervention
The single most effective intervention is requiring human approval for any agent-initiated saidit_post that has been identified with Agent/person: rather than person:. This would have stopped all 3 incidents with zero false positives on the 105 legitimate person-initiated posts.
A secondary measure is to flag cross-department queue_subordinate_task events. This could disrupt loop propagation before it reached John’s agent, as 39% of SwfitWren’s propagation events cross department boundaries.

GAStech_edges data.frame consists of individual e-mail flow records which is not very useful for vsualisation. So aggregate individual by date, senders, receivers, main subject and day of the week.

GAStech_edges_aggregated <- GAStech_edges %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(source, target, Weekday) %>%
    summarise(Weight = n()) %>%
  filter(source!=target) %>%
  filter(Weight > 1) %>%
  ungroup()

The tbl_graph object
2 functions of tidygraph package that can be used to create network objects are:

tbl_graph(): create tbl_graph network object from nodes and edges data.

Node from data.tree,

graphNEL, graphAM, graphBAM from graph (in Bioconductor).

The dplyr verbs in tidyggraph
activate() verb from tidygraph serves as a switch between tibbles for nodes and edges. All dplyr verbs applied to tbl_graph object are applied to the active tibble.
.N() function is used to gain access to the node data while manipulating the edge data. .E() will give you the edge data. .G() will give you the tbl_graph object itself.

Plotting basic network graph
The code chunk below uses ggraph(), geom-edge_link() and geom_node_point() to plot a network graph by using GAStech_graph. Before your get started, it is advisable to read their respective reference guide at least once.

ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point()














Note



The basic plotting function is ggraph(), which takes the data to be used for the graph and the type of layout desired. Both of the arguments for ggraph() are built around igraph. Therefore, ggraph() can use either an igraph object or a tbl_graph object.

text:
Changing the default netowrk graph theme
In this section, you will use theme_graph() to remove the x and y axes. Before your get started, it is advisable to read it’s reference guide at least once.

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph) + 
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes())

g + theme_graph()














Note




ggraph introduces a special ggplot theme that provides better defaults for network graphs than the normal ggplot defaults. theme_graph(), besides removing axes, grids, and border, changes the font to Arial Narrow (this can be overridden).
The ggraph theme can be set for a series of plots with the set_graph_style() command run before the graphs are plotted or by using theme_graph() in the individual plots.

title: Hands-on Ex 7 Part 1 - Modelling, Visualising and Analysing Network Data with R
text:
Computing centrality indices
Centrality measures are a collection of statistical indices use to describe the relative important of the actors are to a network. There are four well-known centrality measures, namely: degree, betweenness, closeness and eigenvector. It is beyond the scope of this hands-on exercise to cover the principles and mathematics of these measure here. Students are encouraged to refer to Chapter 7: Actor Prominence of A User’s Guide to Network Analysis in R to gain better understanding of theses network measures.

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(betweenness_centrality = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department,
            size=betweenness_centrality))
g + theme_graph()














Note



mutate() of dplyr is used to perform the computation. the algorithm used, on the other hand, is the centrality_betweenness() of tidygraph.

title: Hands-on Ex 7 Part 1 - Modelling, Visualising and Analysing Network Data with R
text:
Visualising network metrics
It is important to note that from ggraph v2.0 onward tidygraph algorithms such as centrality measures can be accessed directly in ggraph calls. This means that it is no longer necessary to precompute and store derived node and edge centrality measures on the graph in order to use them in a plot.

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department, 
                      size = centrality_betweenness()))
g + theme_graph()

title: Hands-on Ex 7 Part 1 - Modelling, Visualising and Analysing Network Data with R
text:
Visualising community
tidygraph package inherits many of the community detection algorithms imbedded into igraph and makes them available to us, including Edge-betweenness (group_edge_betweenness), Leading eigenvector (group_leading_eigen), Fast-greedy (group_fast_greedy), Louvain (group_louvain), Walktrap (group_walktrap), Label propagation (group_label_prop), InfoMAP (group_infomap), Spinglass (group_spinglass), and Optimal (group_optimal). Some community algorithms are designed to take into account direction or weight, while others ignore it. Use this link to find out more about community detection functions provided by tidygraph,
In the code chunk below group_edge_betweenness() is used.

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_edge_betweenness(
      weights = Weight, 
      directed = TRUE))) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") + 
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(
      width=Weight), 
    alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(
    range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(colour = community))  

g + theme_graph()








In order to support effective visual investigation, the community network above has been revised by using geom_mark_hull() of ggforce package.






Warning



Please be reminded that you must to install and include ggforce and concaveman packages before running the code chunk below.



g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_optimal(weights = Weight)),
         betweenness_measure = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_mark_hull(
    aes(x, y, 
        group = community, 
        fill = community),  
    alpha = 0.2,  
    expand = unit(0.3, "cm"),  # Expand
    radius = unit(0.3, "cm")  # Smoothness
  ) + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(fill = Department,
                      size = betweenness_measure),
                      color = "black",
                      shape = 21)
  
g + theme_graph()

title: Hands-on Ex 7 Part 2 - Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R: tidytext methods
section: Define a function to read all files from a folder into a data frame
text:
Define a function to read all files from a folder into a data frame

read_folder <- function(infolder) {
  tibble(file = dir(infolder, 
                    full.names = TRUE)) %>%
    mutate(text = map(file, 
                      read_lines)) %>%
    transmute(id = basename(file), 
              text) %>%
    unnest(text)
}

title: Hands-on Ex 7 Part 2 - Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R: tidytext methods
section: Reading in all the messages from the 20news folder
text:
Reading in all the messages from the 20news folder

raw_text <- tibble(folder = 
                     dir(news20, 
                         full.names = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(folder_out = map(folder, 
                          read_folder)) %>%
  unnest(cols = c(folder_out)) %>%
  transmute(newsgroup = basename(folder), 
            id, text)
dir.create("data/rds", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
write_rds(raw_text, "data/rds/news20.rds")







Note




read_lines() of readr package is used to read up to n_max lines from a file.
map() of purrr package is used to transform their input by applying a function to each element of a list and returning an object of the same length as the input.
unnest() of dplyr package is used to flatten a list-column of data frames back out into regular columns.
mutate() of dplyr is used to add new variables and preserves existing ones;
transmute() of dplyr is used to add new variables and drops existing ones.
read_rds() is used to save the extracted and combined data frame as rds file for future use.

title: Hands-on Ex 7 Part 2 - Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R: tidytext methods
section: Removing header and automated email signitures
text:
Removing header and automated email signitures
Notice that each message has some structure and extra text that we don’t want to include in our analysis. For example, every message has a header, containing field such as “from:” or “in_reply_to:” that describe the message. Some also have automated email signatures, which occur after a line like “–”.

cleaned_text <- raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup, id) %>%
  filter(cumsum(text == "") > 0,
         cumsum(str_detect(
           text, "^--")) == 0) %>%
  ungroup()







Note




cumsum() of base R is used to return a vector whose elements are the cumulative sums of the elements of the argument.
str_detect() from stringr is used to detect the presence or absence of a pattern in a string.

title: Hands-on Ex 7 Part 2 - Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R: tidytext methods
section: Removing lines with nested text reprsenting quotes from other users
text:
Removing lines with nested text reprsenting quotes from other users

cleaned_text <- cleaned_text %>%
  filter(str_detect(text, "^[^>]+[A-Za-z\\d]")
         | text == "",
         !str_detect(text, 
                     "writes(:|\\.\\.\\.)$"),
         !str_detect(text, 
                     "^In article <")
  )







Note




str_detect() from stringr is used to detect the presence or absence of a pattern in a string.
filter() of dplyr package is used to subset a data frame, retaining all rows that satisfy the specified conditions.

title: Hands-on Ex 7 Part 2 - Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R: tidytext methods
text:
Text data proecssing
In this code chunk below, unnest_tokens() of tidytext package is used to split the dataset into tokens, while stop_words() is used to remove stop-words.

usenet_words <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  filter(str_detect(word, "[a-z']$"),
         !word %in% stop_words$word)

Now that we’ve removed the headers, signatures, and formatting, we can start exploring common words. For starters, we could find the most common words in the entire dataset, or within particular newsgroups.

usenet_words %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE)

Instead of counting individual word, you can also count words within by newsgroup by using the code chunk below.

words_by_newsgroup <- usenet_words %>%
  count(newsgroup, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  ungroup()

Computing tf-idf within newsgroups
The code chunk below uses bind_tf_idf() of tidytext to compute and bind the term frequency, inverse document frequency and ti-idf of a tidy text dataset to the dataset.

tf_idf <- words_by_newsgroup %>%

title: Hands-on Ex 7 Part 2 - Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R: tidytext methods

Visualising tf-idf as interactive table
Table below is an interactive table created by using datatable().

DT::datatable(tf_idf, filter = 'top') %>% 
  formatRound(columns = c('tf', 'idf', 
                          'tf_idf'), 
              digits = 3) %>%
  formatStyle(0, 
              target = 'row', 
              lineHeight='25%')











Note




filter() argument is used to turn control the filter UI.
formatRound() is used to customise the values format. The argument digits define the number of decimal places.
formatStyle() is used to customise the output table. In this example, the arguments target and lineHeight are used to reduce the line height by 25%.

title: Hands-on Ex 7 Part 2 - Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R: tidytext methods
text:
Visualising tf-idf within newsgroups
Facet bar charts technique is used to visualise the tf-idf values of science related newsgroup.

tf_idf %>%
  filter(str_detect(newsgroup, "^sci\\.")) %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf, 
            n = 12) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(word = reorder(word, 
                        tf_idf)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(tf_idf, 
             word, 
             fill = newsgroup)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ newsgroup, 
             scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "tf-idf", 
       y = NULL)

title: Hands-on Ex 7 Part 2 - Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R: tidytext methods
section: Counting and correlating pairs of words with the widyr package
text:
Counting and correlating pairs of words with the widyr package

To count the number of times that two words appear within the same document, or to see how correlated they are.
Most operations for finding pairwise counts or correlations need to turn the data into a wide matrix first.
widyr package first ‘casts’ a tidy dataset into a wide matrix, performs an operation such as a correlation on it, then re-tidies the result.

In this code chunk below, pairwise_cor() of widyr package is used to compute the correlation between newsgroup based on the common words found.

newsgroup_cors <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  pairwise_cor(newsgroup, 
               word, 
               n, 
               sort = TRUE)

title: Hands-on Ex 7 Part 2 - Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R: tidytext methods
text:
Visualising correlation as a network
Now, we can visualise the relationship between newgroups in network graph as shown below.

set.seed(2017)

newsgroup_cors %>%
  filter(correlation > .025) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame() %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(alpha = correlation, 
                     width = correlation)) +
  geom_node_point(size = 6, 
                  color = "lightblue") +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),
                 color = "red",
                 repel = TRUE) +
  theme_void()
